title: Power Takes the Brakes Off
text:
In 2003 the psychologists Dacher Keltner, Deborah Gruenfeld and Cameron Anderson published an influential theory of how power changes people. They pulled together findings from many experiments and field studies on power, from children in classrooms to managers and animals in dominance hierarchies.

Their argument was that power switches on what psychologists call the approach system. People who hold power have more resources and fewer threats around them, so they tend to feel more positive emotions, notice rewards and opportunities, and act on their impulses. People with little power live with more threats and constraints, so their inhibition system is more active: they are more watchful, more anxious and more attentive to what others think and want.

The theory explained a range of observations. In studies they reviewed, people with more power spoke more freely, interrupted more, judged others more stereotypically and behaved in less inhibited, sometimes rude or socially inappropriate ways, such as eating more greedily from a shared plate. People with less power paid closer attention to others and read them more carefully. The paper became a foundation for a decade of research on what power does to the mind.
lesson: Gaining authority loosens your restraint and dulls your attention to others. The more power you hold, the more deliberately you must listen and check yourself.
people: Dacher Keltner, Deborah Gruenfeld, Cameron Anderson
source: Keltner, D., Gruenfeld, D. H., and Anderson, C. (2003). Power, approach, and inhibition. Psychological Review, 110(2), 265-284.
caveat: It is a theory built from a review of studies; some later findings on specific effects of power have replicated weakly.
